name: Lena Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I coordinate the recruitment team at a pharmaceutical company, so I manage four recruiters who hire lab technicians, warehouse staff and sales reps. My day is checking where every open job is, chasing hiring managers for feedback, reading shortlists and sitting in on a few interviews. I took over the team in March when my boss went on maternity leave and then decided to stay home, so I'm a bit thrown in. I use AI sometimes to write job adverts, because it's quicker than a blank page.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What drives you up the wall in that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hiring managers who don't reply. I can have a perfect candidate for a lab job and lose them because a manager sat on the CV for two weeks. My boyfriend Marco is an electrician and he finds it hilarious how much of my job is sending polite reminders. We bought a flat last year, his parents helped with the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly, because recruiting is about people and I never bought that a robot could judge who'll fit a lab team. At work I'd say let's use the bits that save time and forget the rest. I'm not really an online person, I'd just say it at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad, because I'm still learning to manage and I'd like a few quiet years to get good at it. The one thing that would change is the screening of CVs, which is the most boring bit anyway. My money's fine, I've got eight months saved and Marco's always busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my team as it is and get better at pushing hiring managers. I'd use AI a bit more for adverts and first-round CV sorting, once I've seen it work for a couple of months. And I'd ask for a management course, because I need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI took over the CV screening, what would your recruiters do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to stop thinking of the job as admin and do more of the actual talking to candidates. If the AI only reads the boring CVs, my recruiters finally get to spend their afternoons on the phone with real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that worry you at all, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it'd just be the same job, slightly easier. That's fine by me.

say: I'd say recruiting is about **people** and a machine can't judge fit.
I'd say use the parts that **save time** and forget the rest.
think: She'd be glad of a few **quiet years** to learn to manage.
Only **CV screening** would really change, which is the dull part.
do: Get firmer with **hiring managers** who sit on CVs.
Use AI for **adverts and CV sorting** once it's proven.
S0.quote: If the AI only reads the boring CVs, my recruiters finally get to spend their afternoons on the phone with real people.
fieldNote: She was **thrown into** the role and wants time to grow into it.
Her money feels safe with **eight months** saved and a busy partner.
She'd adopt AI only **after seeing it work** for a while.

steps.text: Ask HR leadership for a management course this year
Trial AI sorting of lab technician CVs for two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say recruitment is changing and we have to change with it. At work I'd be the sensible one saying let's learn it before it's forced on us. I wouldn't panic in public, it's bad for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of my team's work goes: screening, booking interviews, writing offers. That's three of the things on the list. The company could do with two recruiters and a system, and I'm a stand-in manager who's still learning, so I could go either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to pilot the new recruiting software myself, so I'm the person who knows it best. I'd start a part-time certificate in employment law, because disputes and redundancies will need people who understand the rules. And I'd overpay the mortgage a bit less and keep more cash, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying if I said otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be piloting the software that could shrink your team. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I hate that. Because I'd be helping prove we need fewer of us. Learning the recruiting software first might keep my job, but it also makes me the person who shows the company we need fewer recruiters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Marco see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco works with his hands, so he's fine for a long time. It's my half of the mortgage I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and we need a plan, from companies and government both. I wouldn't take sides much, I'd just say people need help to move. With friends I'd be more honest that it's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, recruiting by people is over by 2028. AGI reads CVs, interviews by video and writes the offer before I've had coffee. The odd thing is the company will be firing more people than hiring, so the work that's left is helping people leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into outplacement, that's helping people who've been made redundant find new jobs, because there'll be a mountain of it for a while. I'd cut our spending, so no new kitchen. And I'd rely on Marco's work while I switch, which he'd be fine with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My heart's going a bit just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would the outplacement work last, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a couple of years, and I'd use them. My boyfriend Marco fixes wiring for a living, so for three years he's the safe one and I'm the one who needs a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we're a team, and he'd mean it. But I've always paid my half, and I'd hate not to.

I'd admit to **friends** that it's scary.
think: The work left is **helping people leave**, not hiring.
The company would be **firing more** people than it hires.

fieldNote: She spots a **short-lived niche** in helping people who've been laid off.

steps.text: Apply for outplacement adviser jobs helping laid-off staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if companies are straight with people. I'd want our HR team to tell staff early which jobs change. That's the practical thing I'd push for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got a few good years in recruiting, and then I'd need to be somewhere else. The part of HR I think lasts longest is the messy human stuff: disputes, grievances, people crying in meeting rooms. Nobody wants a robot telling them they've lost their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the employment law certificate and then train in workplace mediation. I'd keep using the AI tools in recruiting, so I'm useful while the job lasts. By year three or four I'd move into employee relations at the same company or another pharma firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will mediation need people when AGI can do the thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and I've thought about that. The last job in HR will be sitting with someone on the worst day of their working life, and I think I'd actually be good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32. Marco and I talked about kids at around 30, and I'd want to be in the new job before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we can do this sensibly. I'd want schools and companies preparing people now, not in year nine. Pretty middle-of-the-road, that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel quite lucky in this one. I'd be 37, with Marco's trade, the flat nearly half paid off and a decade to move. It still means recruiting ends, but I'd have a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep recruiting for a few years and get properly good at it, and with the AI. Then I'd move into employee relations or mediation around year five. And we'd have our first child around 30 as planned, because ten years means we don't have to put our lives on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it doesn't take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your family comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's dad. He's a plumber, 60, and he'd love not working past 65. Ten years means my boyfriend's dad (a plumber of 60) retires before the robots arrive, and that's the one nice thought in all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any guilt in feeling lucky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, more than I'd admit at work. I'd worry about the people with no flat and no partner in a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Recruiters would be one of the first things to go and I'd be learning a new job in a panic. What would help is companies being honest early and paying for people to train, and some kind of wage support while you switch. I can change jobs, I've done it before, but I need more than a month's notice to become a different person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people we hire. I put lab technicians and warehouse staff into jobs, and I'd want to know their jobs last too. That part I didn't get to say.

headlineQuote: I can change jobs, I've done it before, but I need more than a month's notice to become a different person.
portrait: Lena is **27** and stands in as manager of four recruiters at a pharmaceutical company.
She uses **AI now and then** for adverts and adopts tools once they're proven.
She owns a flat with her boyfriend Marco, an **electrician**, and has eight months saved.
As AGI gets closer she'd move from recruiting into **outplacement** or **employee relations**.
She sees the **human side** of HR, like disputes and bad news, as the last to go.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, learning a new job in a **panic**.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being **honest early** and paying for training.
